title: Educational psychology
content:
• A branch of psychology dealing with teaching and learning is referred to as Educational Psychology. When said simply, it is the application of findings of psychology in the educational field.
• Educational psychology is the systematic study of individual development in educational settings.
• It is related to learning processes and psychological aspects in teaching and learning of students.

Scope
• Educational psychology covers a wider scope. It is concerned with different areas of educational processes.
• It comprises the learner, learning process and evaluation systems.

The learner
• The learner specific area of educational psychology deals with treating learner as a unique individual. The learner is understood in terms of growth and development, as well as individual difference – including those of personality, individual difference, aptitude and related characteristics.
• The understanding of learner is important for a teacher to identify student’s problems and adopt strategies and methods to address them. In addition, knowledge of the learner help teacher to create a supportive learning environment within institutions, where every student is encouraged to develop their inherent potential. A teacher should be aware of the behavioural tendencies/ patterns of the students at particular ages and their problems associated with psychological characteristics. This knowledge equips the teacher to assist the learner effectively.

Learning process
It reveals how students learn. It pertains to laws and principles of learning and mainly comprise the theories of learning.
Educational psychology provides knowledge of the learning process. This helps teachers to modify teaching process for better outcomes. It emphasizes the use of appropriate teaching strategies and learning theories to establish an effective communication in classroom. By recognizing different approaches, teachers can organize instructions suitable for classroom needs. Thus, it equips teacher to cultivate a distraction free and attentive classroom environment for students.

Evaluation systems
Evaluation of learning process in educational psychology involves a systematic collection and interpretation of evidence to determine the effectiveness of teaching, learning and curriculum. It furnishes feedbacks to both teachers and learners.
Evaluation assesses whether the learning objectives are attained or not. It assesses the teaching innovations brought up by teacher, thereby helping the teacher to reflect upon their practices and methods. The psychological tests like intelligent tests, aptitude tests, achievement test helps to identify strength, weaknesses and difficulties of learners. This informs teachers to make decision on guiding and supporting learners. Evaluation and assessment provide immediate feedback that motivates both learners and teachers promoting positive actions.

Importance of Educational psychology
• Helps in determining the aims and objectives of education
• Assist in planning of curriculum
• Helps in adopting suitable teaching and learning methods
• Foster the knowledge about nature and behaviour of child.
• Provide knowledge to carry out evaluation procedures
• Assist in solving the classroom problems effectively
• Helps in recognizing individual difference and respond them effectively

The most simple definition of educational psychology is the application of psychological finding in the field of education. Educational psychology is the systematic study of the development of the individual within the educational setting. It helps the teacher to foster harmonious overall development of the student.

Relationship of Psychology and Education
Psychology as a behavioural science aims to study the behaviour. Behaviour is an action which can be seen and observed in an objective way. The basic aim of education is to modify behaviour. Any modification of behaviour presupposes a knowledge of the development of behaviour. Psychology as a science helps to understand, control and predict behaviour. Psychologists, through scientific descriptions of human behaviour and the organic and emotional requirement of the human organism, have had a profound influence upon the objectives of education.
The goal of education is to help the individual become increasingly self-directive. The teachers have a unique responsibility for teaching certain types of knowledge, skills and developing certain attitudes.
Educational psychology must also include study of problems of teaching and learning, besides the learning process. Therefore, the science most basic to education is psychology. The teacher needs psychology to bridge the lives of the young and meet the aims of education. To be a successful teacher one also needs to understand the learners, just as to be a successful nurse you are required to have professional knowledge and skill as well as the knowledge about the nature of the patient

SCOPE OF EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY
Educational psychology has a vast scope because it is concerned with the education process. It deals with transmission of knowledge, nurturance of social and personal development and enhancement of motor and artistic skills. This educative process in a broad sense is a life long process. We shall now focus on the specific areas where educational psychology has very important applications, namely,
i) Learner,
ii) Learning Process, and
iii) Evaluation of learning performance.

1.3.1 Learner
The success of education depends on adapting teaching to individual differences among learners. Educational psychology helps in understanding the developmental characteristics of the students, their individual differences related to intelligence and personality, their adjustment abilities and their attitudes towards learning. Each learner is an unique individual with different abilities, interests, ways of thinking and responding, thus these characteristics have a significant influence on ones learning styles.
It is being realized that students use different learning strategies. They have different methods of reading, interpreting and coding the information. Sometimes these strategies are useful but some students also develop pathological learning strategies. The teachers should help their students to learn to successfully control their cognitive processes including learning to learn, to remember and to think. In order to successfully pursue the goal of teaching students how to learn, it is useful to understand the learning process i.e. what goes on in the learner’s head during learning. To instruct effectively in the class, the teacher must understand her students, their problems and methods to modify the problem.
With the help of educational psychology teachers are able to understand individual differences and may adjust teaching to the needs and requirements of the class. He/she may also study the factors which are responsible for individual differences. He/she may be helpful in creating conducive environments in the schools/teaching institutions where the students can develop their inherent potentialities to the maximum.
Good mental health is very important for efficient learning. The teacher from the study of psychology can know the various factors which are responsible for the mental ill health and maladjustments. As a teacher one may understand the causes of the problems of children which occur at different age levels and can successfully solve them. There is a great difference in the method of solving problems of children by a trained teacher. The teacher who is familiar with the fundamental principles of human behaviour applies his knowledge of educational psychology to solve and prevent problems.
Development of positive attitudes is also very important for effective learning and teaching process. Thus the knowledge gained here would help to develop positive attitudes towards profession and as a prospective teacher this would provide you with the necessary competencies to meet the classroom challenges. With this knowledge you can increase your student’s motivation and change negative attitudes which interfere with the learning process.
It has been recognized that personality factors contribute something beyond intellectual abilities to perform an academic task. Personality needs of the individual are of major importance to learning readiness. Studies have consistently shown the importance of the individual’s value system and the controlling influence of intrinsic motivation on learning. Although it is now been shown that student does not receive stimulus from teacher alone, but selects information which best meets with his need and as per his values.
Although there have been numerous personality factors related to academic achievement but main focus has been on academic motivation and its constituents-achievements motivation, anxiety, self-concepts and locus of control. Among the most replicated results are findings concerning school-related anxiety, which show a curvilinear relationship between anxiety and performance i.e. poor performance with too little or no anxiety and also when it is too high particularly when short-term memory demands are there (Sarason, 1980). Lens (1983) has demonstrated the same inverted U-shaped relationship for both test anxiety and need for achievement. Weiner (1979) has shown in several experiments that the manner in which academic performances are interpreted by individuals has a strong influence on subjective statements of affect, motivated behaviour towards tasks, and actual task performance. Internal attributions for success generate positive affect, increased effort towards tasks, and greater higher performance expectations.
Some investigations have been in actual classroom contexts with teachers and students. The results have shown that poor performance patterns are often the results of interactions among classroom performance demands, lowered coping capabilities (including factors like increased anxiety and lowered efficacy expectations that reflect unfavourable self-assessments of ability), and lower levels of intellectual ability (Clifford, 1979; Schunk, 1994).
Knowledge of educational psychology would help to reduce performance demands for lower ability students who appear less able to cope with traditional instruction.

1.3.2 Learning Process
Learning process is how the student learns. The knowledge of educational psychology provides the knowledge of learning process in general and problems of classroom learning in particular. Our daily experiences indicate that some teacher are successful in the classroom than others. Some communicate very effectively subject-matter in the class to students and some fail irrespective of their knowledge of the subject matter. Success depends on something other than the subject. The knowledge of principles of behaviour helps to understand the behaviour of students one teaches, the developmental characteristics, their abilities, an influence and contribution of heredity and environment in the process of development of an individual’s personality. To instruct effectively in the class, the teacher must understand the principles of learning and various approaches to the learning process, problems of learning and their remedial measures. It also gives the knowledge of various approaches to understand the learning process, factors affecting and guidance for effective learning.
For effective outcome and performance with knowledge of learning process, one can modify the method of teaching and learning. Lack of proper methods of teaching sometimes results in failure of communication in the classroom. Educational psychology gives us the knowledge of appropriate methods of teaching. It helps in developing new strategies of teaching. It is related to and uses several theories of teaching-learning. The teacher must be acquainted with the knowledge of various theories in order to organise his classroom teaching. Educational psychology provides us with the knowledge of different approaches evolved to tackle the problems of teaching at different age levels. The learning environment should be such that distractions are minimized, attention of the learners could be sustained for optimum period of time.
Psychological principles are also used in formulating curriculum for different stages. Needs of the students, their developmental characteristics, learning patterns and needs of the society, all these are to be incorporated in the curriculum. The curriculum in recent years includes the needs of the individual and society so that maximum transfer may occur from school to social situations.
Another important contribution of educational psychology is the provision and organisation of the special education for the exceptional children (handicapped).

1.3.3 Evaluation of Learning Process
With the help of psychological tests learning outcomes or curriculum, course content can be evaluated. Measurement of aptitudes and any innovations introduced in teaching by the teacher should also be evaluated, as an immediate feedback and knowledge of results enhances learner’s motivation. Evaluation is also important for research studies.

title: Growth and Development
content:
• Growth and development are changes occurring in human beings from conception to death. Even though these two concepts are often used interchangeably, they differ from each other.
• Development is the gradual change in structure, function, and behavior that occurs in an orderly way and remains reasonably stable for a longer period of life.
• Growth refers to physical changes in the body, such as changes in height and weight, that occur up to a particular time in the lifespan.

### Comparison: Growth vs. Development
• Nature: Growth is quantitative in nature; Development is qualitative in nature.
• Duration: Growth occurs or continues up to a particular period in life; Development is a continuous and lifelong process.
• Scope (Physical vs. Functional): Growth is confined to physical changes (e.g., increase in the size of hand and fingers); Development is not confined to physical changes and involves functional changes (e.g., writing with the help of the hand).
• Aspects Involved: Growth is mainly physical and biological; Development involves cognitive, emotional, social, and moral aspects.
• Measurement: Precise measurement of growth is possible via visible physical metrics (e.g., height/weight in cm/m); Development is assessed indirectly through behavior and functionality, meaning not all changes are directly visible.

### Relationship Between Growth and Development
• Growth generally leads to development, but this does not occur automatically or always.
• Development can occur independently and is not strictly dependent on growth.

### Examples Illustrating Growth vs. Development
• A child's brain grows in size and complexity – Growth
• It leads to improved thinking, memory, etc. – Development
• A teenager grows muscle mass – Growth
• ...but may not develop emotional maturity or social responsibility – Development
• A child improves in problem-solving and wisdom – Development
• ...even though he is a dwarf or physical growth has stopped – Growth

title: Principles of Development
content:
### Principles of Development
• Development is continuous: It is a continuous process starting from conception and continuing till death. Changes happen in a connected and gradual manner rather than in sudden steps.
• Development is gradual: It is not an abrupt process; it progresses steadily and consistently.
• Development occurs sequentially: Development follows a logical order. Although changes vary for each individual due to individual differences, the sequence flows systematically from infancy to old age or late adulthood.
• Development proceeds from general to specific: Children initially respond to the outer environment in general terms (e.g., using a common sound or word for all objects) before proceeding to use specific words for each distinct object.
• Development depends on individual differences: While the general pattern of development is common, each individual develops in their own way based on heredity and environmental factors. Development is not uniform; children born at the same time may show varied timelines in acquiring skills like language.
• Development is predictable: Although the rate of development varies, it is predictable because it follows a general pattern and direction. Predicting children's behavior at certain stages is possible since development occurs through ordered stages with specific characteristics.
• Development exhibits interrelatedness: Development encompasses multiple dimensions—physical, cognitive, emotional, social, and moral. A balanced interrelation connects all aspects (e.g., brain maturation supports cognitive development, while emotional connectedness enhances social behavior).
• Development is influenced by heredity and environment: A child develops through both inherited traits and acquired traits from the environment. If the environment fails to support an inherited trait, it cannot develop to its full potential (e.g., a child born with musical talent who lacks encouragement may set that talent aside).
• Development is an integration of all dimensions: An individual is an integration of all developmental dimensions rather than a single-dimensional representation. Different skills and abilities come together and work as one (e.g., early separate actions like seeing, reaching, and grasping later integrate into the coordinated activity of picking up an object).

### Aspects of Human Development
• Physical development: Dealing with changes in the body and physical structure.
• Personal development: Dealing with transformations in an individual's identity and personality.
• Social development: Dealing with adjustments one makes to relate to others and society.
• Cognitive development: Changes in the way one thinks, reasons, and makes decisions.

title: Stages of development
content:
Stage: Prenatal | Time period: Conception to birth | Characteristics: -

Stage: Infancy and toddlerhood | Time period: Birth to 2 years | Characteristics:
Period of rapid growth and development.
The infant cries most the time for satisfying hunger and sleeps after it as routine.
Infant depends mostly on mothers.
At initial stages exhibit simple muscular movements and develops coordinated movements.
After attaining motor balance of head, they start to move with lower body.
Child display self-assertion and demand everything child needed in environment.
Child focus on gratification of needs and not aware of social norms

Stage: Early childhood | Time period: 3 – 7 years | Characteristics:
Also called preschool stage
Refinement of behaviour and social interaction of child take place.
Cognitive abilities and language abilities shows a significant development
Socially child is cooperative and love learning, playing and growing with others

Stage: Later childhood | Time period: 7-12 years | Characteristics:
Marked by moral, intellectual and social development.
Child form peer groups and interact more with children of same gender.
Child began to know about rules and norms and start to obey them
Motor coordination improves a lot.

Stage: Adolescence | Time period: 13- 18 years | Characteristics:
It is the transitional stage from childhood to mature individuals.
The individuals here are treated neither as child nor adult, but in between them.
The stage is marked by major emotional, physical, cognitive and societal changes.
Sexual maturation happens in this stage with desire for opposite sex
The stage is marked by increased self-consciousness.
Peer groups are highly influential in this stage.
They gain thinking capabilities logically and abstractly
Stage is characterised by a period of stress and storm

Stage: Adulthood | Time period: Age after 18 | Characteristics:
Mature stage of increased responsibilities and roles.
Early adulthood Individual focuses on career development, planning for the future and ready to get married.
In the later adulthood, individuals take care of family responsibilities, taking care of children, guiding people with their experiences.
The final phase, called old age, prepares individual for retirement life. As individuals grow older the concern for health increased due to gradual declination of bodily functions. The individuals prepare for the end of the life period.

title: Brain
content:
Brain – structure and function
For understanding how learning and behaviour occur in humans, it is important to understand the structure of human body. In relation to educational psychology more attention is given to structures like brain and neurons. These structures support cognition, emotions and actions. They influence on individuals learning, processing experiences and responding to environment, thereby are essential components in teaching and learning.

Brain consists of 80% water along with other fats and protein. Brain consists of two hemispheres right and the left. Cerebral cortex is the largest part of brain covering the cerebrum. Cerebral cortex has 4 parts called lobes as frontal lobe, parietal lobe, temporal lobe and occipital lobe.

Parts of brain and Functions:
- Parts of brain: Brain stem | Functions: Heartrate, breathing, blood pressure, sleeping, wakeful attention
- Parts of brain: Cerebellum | Functions: Balance and smooth skilled movements
- Parts of brain: Hippocampus | Functions: Recalling new information and recent experiences
- Parts of brain: Amygdala | Functions: Emotions and aggression
- Parts of brain: Corpus callosum | Functions: Connects two hemispheres of brain
- Parts of brain: Frontal lobe | Functions: Planning, remembering, decision making, thinking creatively, problem solving
- Parts of brain: Parietal lobe | Functions: Processing sensory information
- Parts of brain: Temporal lobe | Functions: Hearing and memory
- Parts of brain: Occipital lobe | Functions: Vision

When any damage is caused to right side of brain, it affects the movement of left side of the body and vice versa. Left hemisphere of brain is prominent part in language processing. right hemisphere handles visual spatial information and emotions.

Brain imaging techniques:
- Name: CAT scan (Computerized Axial Tomography) | Functionality: Provide 3-D images of brain using x ray technology | Limitations: Provide less information about brain activity; Cannot be repeatedly done due to radiation exposure
- Name: PET scan (Positron Emission Tomography) | Functionality: Shows the brain activities. The radioactive glucose injected is consumed by areas of brain performing varied activities. High activity needs high glucose level and displayed as brighter color on computerized maps | Limitations: Due to radio active injection, it is not feasible for more sessions.
- Name: EEG (Electroencephalograph) | Functionality: Record electrical activity in brain produced by neural signals. The electrodes attached to scalp display the pattern of the electrical activity | Limitations: Does not provide pictures of the brain. Make available the activity of brain, but fails to tell location of activity
- Name: ERP (Event Related Potentials) | Functionality: Perform calculations EEG data based on the brain's response to stimulus. | Limitations: Not good at identifying the place where activity is occurring.
- Name: fMRI (Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging) | Functionality: Provide the blood flow within the brain associated with activity. It conveys the work needed for certain stimuli. | Limitations: A brief lag is displayed in changes in brain activity and changes in blood flow
- Name: NIR -OT ( Near -infrared Optical Tomography) | Functionality: Use of optical fibre to pass near infrared light through the brain. The reflected light exposing the blood flow and oxygenation reports the brain activity. | Limitations: The near infrared light can penetrate and show activity within few centimetres of brain.

title: Neurons
content:
Neurons
Nerve cells - Specialized nerve cells transmitting information across brain and to parts of nervous system.
Neurons are brain’s grey matter as they are grey in colour. One neuron has its information capacity resemble to a computer.
Dendrites and axons are crucial parts of a neuron.
Dendrites are short, branched parts which receive messages and bring them inside the cell body.
Axon is long, slender part that carries messages from away from body. Axon is embodied with myeline sheaths which accelerates the transmission of messages through it.
The tiny spaces between neurons are called synapses.
Synapses are filled with glial cells which are called as the white matte of the brain, glial cells help in fighting infections, provide myelin coating and control blood flow as well as neuron communication.
Through electrical signals the neurons share information and it is carried to each neurons through synapses through neurotransmitters. These synaptic transmissions become stronger by repeated use and weaker by when not in use. Thus the strength of synaptic connections is dynamic.
The child during earlier stages are oversupplied with neurons and neurons which are used mostly develop unused neurons are pruned. This pruning is important for cognitive development as it keeps brain more organized and efficient.

Brain development
Brain development occurs throughout the childhood and adolescence.
Infants recognize the patterns in their world and languages spoken by the caretakers. Through observation, exploration and acting they form neural connection and learn. At this stage they are self-directed and as a teacher or care taker the best thing we can do is to provide a stimulating, responding and safe environment.
Brains of young children have more plasticity. In elementary school period parts of the brain supporting memory, perception, emotions grow and become connected.
During adolescence period the limbic system develops earlier supporting emotions, risk taking, novelty characteristics in adolescence.
As the prefrontal lobe involving decision making and judgement develops later the limbic system, the adolescents tend to be pleasure seekers and adventures for immediate thrills at early adolescence period and become mature decision makers on their actions and adventures during later stages to become adult.
Adolescents brain is described as high horse powers with poor steering. By the development of prefrontal lobes at later on make them handling their power effectively.
Culture also has role in shaping brain plasticity. Children of China retain a visual motor sense of numbers due to their practice in abacus using arithmetic teaching. Brain is ever changing and shaped by contexts and cultures.

Myths about brain:
- Myths: You use only 10% of brain | Truth: You use all your brain
- Myths: Some people are more right brained and some others left brained | Truth: It takes both sides to do the things
- Myths: We can’t change our brain | Truth: Out brain is constantly changing all the time
Source: Based on Aamodt & Wang (2008); K. W. Fischer (2009); Freeman (2011); OECD (2007).
Anita Woolfolk & Preeti Kapur. Educational Psychology, 14e (p. 52). Pearson Education. Kindle Edition.

Implication in teaching:
- Understanding brain functioning help in making aware about cognitive process and then developing educational practices based on it.
- Notion of education is to using of brain for changing of brain by embracing plasticity for better performance.
- Learning through multiple ways can tackle the brain’s inherent limitation.
- Changing the brain takes time, so gradual and consistent practice and compassionate in teaching and reteaching is needed.
- Learning should be connected with concrete experience so that learner can develop good connections and network. Brain seeks meaningful pattern from existing networks
- Feedback is necessary to correct the networks to learn
- Help students to understand that the changing of their own brain requires personal responsibility, effort and learning.
